description:
Hey there we are OuterX, 

A team participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge and aiming to contribute towards NASA's mission.

Our goal is to explore ways to improve how astronauts’ health is monitored during space missions. We believe that taking care of the people who explore space is just as important as exploring space itself, and we’re excited to contribute our ideas and skills to this challenge.
summary:
Last Signal is an interactive web story that retells NASA’s Spirit rover mission in five short chapters, from its landing at Gusev Crater in 2004 to its last contact in 2010. Each chapter pairs an imagined first-person journal entry, written as if Spirit were speaking, with the real science from NASA and JPL. Players answer one question in each of the first four chapters to recover an evidence clue, and finishing all four earns a printable mission certificate.
The story is built around a failure. In 2006, Spirit’s right front wheel stopped turning. As the rover dragged it through the soil, it exposed bright, silica rich material, which scientists concluded was likely formed through a process involving water. We chose this moment because it shows how science really works: a setback became a discovery, and the conclusion stayed careful. The silica points to ancient water, not to life.
Every claim links back to a NASA source, and the project states clearly that it is independent and not affiliated with NASA. It runs in any browser, includes a read-aloud option, and is designed for ages 10 and up.
details:
What it does and how it works

Last Signal is a browser-based interactive story about NASA’s Spirit rover. Players move through five chapters, from the 2004 landing to the end of the mission. Each chapter shows a NASA image, an imagined journal entry from Spirit, and a “real science” panel with a link to the NASA source. The first four chapters end with a three option question. A correct answer recovers an evidence clue and fills a progress meter, and a wrong answer points the player back to the science note so they can try again. Recovering all four clues unlocks a printable mission certificate with the player’s name. Progress is saved in the browser, so players can leave and come back.

Benefits and intended impact

Students learn what Spirit did and also how scientists reason from evidence. The silica question teaches the difference between “evidence of ancient water” and “proof of life,” a distinction that is easy to get wrong. We want students to see that hardware left behind on Mars still teaches us things, and that a failure like the broken wheel can become a discovery.


Tools and technology

We built the project with HTML, CSS, and plain JavaScript, with no frameworks or backend. The rover on the welcome screen is an inline SVG illustration we drew. The images come from NASA and JPL’s public image resources, which load directly from NASA’s servers, and each one is credited and linked to its source. The read aloud feature uses the browser’s built-in speech synthesis, and the certificate uses a print stylesheet. Nothing is sent to a server, so the project collects no personal data.

We used AI assistance to help write and refine the project descriptions and to improve grammar. The story, the science content, and the design choices are our own, and we checked every science claim against NASA sources.
